name: Photodynamic therapy (ALA-PDT)
lead: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) uses a light-sensitive drug (photosensitizer) and light of a suitable wavelength to produce reactive oxygen species that kill targeted cells.[1] In ALA-PDT, aminolevulinic acid (ALA), a precursor in the body's heme synthesis, is applied so that cells accumulate the photosensitizer protoporphyrin IX before light is shone on the area.[1]

Dermatologically it is best established for actinic keratosis and certain skin cancers.[1] For acne it has been studied mainly in severe or inflammatory acne. A 2016 systematic review described it as safe and effective for acne, while one phase II trial found it no better than blue or violet light alone, according to a general reference.[1] Reported side effects in acne treatment include marked redness, moderate to severe pain and burning.[1]

paras: A photosensitizer collects in the target tissue and is activated by light, passing energy to oxygen and producing singlet oxygen and other reactive species that damage cell membranes and proteins; because damage occurs only where light is applied, the effect stays localised.[1] ALA is a prodrug that causes protoporphyrin IX to build up faster than cells convert it to heme; it peaks within hours and clears in about a day, which limits skin sensitivity.[1] Methyl and other esterified forms improve bioavailability for skin use.[1]

Early work in the late 1800s and early 1900s in Hermann von Tappeiner's laboratory showed that light, a dye and oxygen together were toxic, and he coined the term photodynamic action. Clinical development in the 1970s, including work by Thomas Dougherty, helped establish PDT, and Photofrin became the first approved PDT agent in 1993.[1]

In appearance communities ALA-PDT is mentioned as a clinician-administered option for severe or treatment-resistant acne, usually alongside discussion of lasers and isotretinoin. It requires a medical provider.
The main side effect of PDT is skin photosensitivity, and in acne treatment it can cause marked redness, moderate to severe pain and burning.[1]

A randomized, investigator-blinded trial in 15 patients with at least 12 facial inflammatory acne lesions compared ALA-PDT with methyl aminolevulinate (MAL)-PDT for treatment effect and tolerability.[2] A 2016 systematic review called PDT safe and effective for acne, while one phase II trial found no advantage over blue or violet light alone, according to a general reference.[1]
Other cited ALA-PDT studies concern actinic keratosis, Bowen disease, basal cell carcinoma and other non-acne conditions, so they do not speak to acne.[3]

timeline.event: Hermann von Tappeiner's laboratory describes photodynamic action.[1]
Thomas Dougherty's clinical work helps establish PDT.[1]
Photofrin becomes the first approved PDT agent.[1]

lore.intro: ALA-PDT is discussed as a clinic procedure for severe acne when other treatments have not worked.[1]

claims.claim: ALA-PDT can clear severe or inflammatory acne.
claims.believers: Proponents point to clinic results and small trials showing reduced inflammatory lesions.[2]
claims.experts: A 2016 systematic review called PDT safe and effective for acne, but one phase II trial found it no better than blue or violet light alone.[1]

claims.claim: The procedure is painful and leaves skin red for days.
claims.believers: Users describe burning and redness during and after treatment.[1]
claims.experts: Reference sources list marked redness, moderate to severe pain and burning as side effects in acne treatment.[1]

card.summary: Photosensitizer plus light for severe acne; some trials and a review are positive, but results are mixed and treatment is painful.
card.note: Clinician-administered; pain, redness and photosensitivity are common.

quick.overview:
ALA-PDT applies aminolevulinic acid to the skin and then light, which kills targeted cells. It is established for actinic keratosis and some skin cancers and has been studied for severe acne.

A 2016 review called it safe and effective for acne, while one phase II trial found no advantage over blue or violet light alone.
quick.mechanism: ALA makes cells accumulate protoporphyrin IX, which on light exposure produces reactive oxygen species that damage the treated cells.
quick.risks: Marked redness, moderate to severe pain, burning and photosensitivity are reported. It is performed by clinicians.
